title: Ashaveri Evidence Pack (JSON twin of the CBOR/COSE container)
description: Display-only projection of the signed COSE_Sign1 pack container. The CBOR bytes are canonical; this JSON form is never signed directly. Byte strings appear as lowercase hex, which is how the receipt's own projection writes them, and a length that is a number of bytes in the CBOR is not the same measure as a JSON string length, so only `minLength` on an id carries a bound the framing states and nothing else here pretends to. Closure is not the manifest's alone: the manifest map and every map it opens, `span`, `chain`, `duty`, each entry of `items`, each entry of `custody` with the key and the window inside it, and each entry of `attached`, name their members in the same object, which is where `additionalProperties` applies, so a member the format does not define is refused at that level rather than read and dropped on the way to a verifier. `protectedHeader` carries the three labels the CDDL declares and no more, and this definition carries no closure keyword: that map is read by number, its bytes are what the signature hashes, and a document carrying a fourth label is refused before any projection of it is built. The envelope above it is projected more loosely than the format writes it, and that is a decision rather than a gap: this document requires `protectedHeader` and `payload`, names `signature` without demanding it, and leaves its own root unclosed, so a pack shown before it is signed still shows, while `pack.cddl` requires all four elements of the `COSE_Sign1` and sixty-four bytes in the fourth of them. Requiring the missing one here would refuse a display and not an artifact, which is the same reason the receipt's projection is written the same way. The CBOR tag that wraps the four elements on the wire, tag 18, is stated in `pack.cddl` and cannot be stated here at all, because a JSON object has no tag to carry: a reader who needs the bytes needs the format, and that is where the number is. `art` is not an enum here because the retention-duty registry is a reader's question rather than this file's, which is also why the CDDL writes it `tstr`: a label the reader cannot interpret is refused by the reader that knows the registry, and a format that listed the labels it happens to know would decide a legal question it cannot check. `a` is an enum here because the two arms a document can have been weighed by are the format's own answer and nothing a reader looks up. No member states whether the duty was met, and that is the format's decision rather than an omission: a reader holding `at`, `held` and `required` answers it in one comparison, and a conclusion the deployment signed about itself is worth less as evidence than the three integers are. The rules that hold between two members are not spelled out here because no keyword reaches them: that every item's stamp lies inside the span, that the end of the span is no later than the instant assembly began, that the revision the period came from precedes it, that the seconds held are at least the age of the oldest receipt in this pack, that no two items answer to one `id`, that every item of the array is reached from the anchor, that every reference answers for exactly one `held` slot of one sealed receipt and every slot that states material is answered by exactly one reference, that the instants a reference states are whole numbers of Unix seconds inside the band the receipt format states, that every attached entry states the digest its own bytes hash to and no digest is attached twice, that an attached entry resolves to the reference whose body digest it is and carries a header only where that reference states a digest for one, and that either list and each entry of it lie under the ceilings the format takes from its own contents, and that no instant lies before the epoch and no duration below zero, are all stated in `pack.cddl`, which is where a reader holding this projection has to go to learn them. Nothing in this repository decides what a pack is assembled from, and `packages/receipt/src/pack.ts` both writes these bytes and reads them back, so this definition and `pack.cddl` are the layout that writer is held to and the one a second implementation can be measured against.

kid.description: sha256 of the Ed25519 public key, hex

typ.description: the content type that tells a pack apart from a receipt, which the same key signs

payload.description: The signed manifest, and the only part of a pack a verifier has to believe before it starts walking. Exactly one version is defined, so `v` is a constant rather than a discriminant, and a document naming another version is not this one.

signature.description: Ed25519 signature over the Sig_structure, hex

at.description: unix seconds, the instant assembly began, stamped before the reads so a slow store cannot date a pack later than the window it describes

span.description: the period the pack answers for, half-open: `from` included, `to` excluded

chain.description: the two endpoints a reader walks between, neither of them derivable from the items

duty.description: the retention duty the pack answers, and the revision of the mapping the required period was read from

items.description: The receipts, at least one. Order in this array carries nothing: a reader follows each item's `prev` to find its predecessor, because retiring a prefix rewrites the front of a chain without touching a surviving record's digest, and the item whose `prev` is the anchor is first while the one whose own digest is the head is last. A pack of nothing would have no first item, so its walk would be vacuous, which is why `minItems` is one and not a courtesy.

custody.description: What the sealed receipts' `held` slots answer for: one reference per named slot, stating the origin read, the request as asked, the identity the document named for itself, the instant its last byte landed and what that source declares about itself, the body digest, the chain digest, the arm that weighed it and the window it signed for itself. It carries no floor, because an empty list is the pack saying it refers to nothing and every sealed slot of such a pack states an absence: an absent member and an empty list are two different claims. No entry of it carries vendor content, and no entry carries a verdict, because whether the material a reference names verifies is settled by the roots a reader stands behind at an instant of its own asking. Resolution is by the slot a sealed receipt names and by nothing else, since a second name for one digest is the thing that drifts, and the two ceilings this member carries, the count of references against the two slots per item and the length of a request, are stated in `pack.cddl` because no keyword here reaches either side of a length.

attached.description: The byte arm: material a deployment attaches beside the references, whole, for the one case the terms of the service that answered allow it, which is a deployment holding rights to hand those particular bytes on. It carries no floor, and an empty list is this pack attaching nothing, which is what every pack a deployment of this estate assembles states: the layout permits the arm and no path a deployment runs fills it, because what decides whether a deployment may redistribute what it holds is its own agreement with the service and not a question this container answers. An entry resolves to exactly one reference, by the digest its own bytes hash to beside that reference's body digest, and each digest is recomputed by the reader rather than believed.

manifest.description: A pack manifest and nothing else. The map is closed: a member outside this list is a malformed pack rather than a member a reader agreed to forget, and the same holds of every map below it. `custody` and `attached` stand where one member did: the reference list answers for each held slot, and the arm holds material only where a deployment attaches it.

to.description: unix seconds, excluded: a receipt issued at exactly this stamp belongs to the next pack

span.description: The half-open interval the store served, which is the bound the store's own range query uses. The walk shows that nothing between the first item and the last is missing; this is what shows a reader whether the run they are reading is the period they asked for.

anchor.description: the digest the first item was chained from: thirty-two zero bytes before any retirement, otherwise the seam a trim record carried

head.description: the digest of the last item in the chain

chain.description: Both endpoints inside the signature, which is what gives the walk its meaning. An anchor a reader invented would let a deployment start the walk wherever it liked and a head read off the last item handed over would let it stop there, so a run of receipts the reader was never shown would go unseen. Publishing the head is what makes deletion detectable.

art.description: a label from the retention-duty registry, which this estate reads as "19(1)", "19(2)" and "26(6)". Not an enum here because the CDDL admits any tstr: the reader that knows the registry refuses a label outside it, and 19(2) and 26(6) route a financial institution's logs into applicable Union financial-services law, which this format does not interpret.

rev.description: unix seconds, the revision of the mapping `required` was read from. The member that makes the other three readable later: a claim made in 2027 is read against the revision it was made from, not against whatever the mapping says the day the artifact is opened.

required.description: seconds that revision of the mapping required, which is the deployment's to state and this format supplies no default for

held.description: seconds the store has held the oldest receipt it still retains, measured at `at`. Not derivable from the items, which is the only reason it is stated: a pack covers one span and the duty runs against everything retained.

duty.description: The duty, the period, the revision the period came from, and the time actually held. Whether the duty was met is absent on purpose: a reader comparing `held` with `required` answers it, and an artifact that states the conclusion beside the evidence invites a reader to stop checking the numbers.

id.description: the store's own id for the receipt, as the record names it. The framing bounds it at 65535 bytes and an empty id belongs to a trim record, which is never an item; `minLength` is the half of that a JSON length can state, and the CBOR is where the byte bound is read.

iat.description: unix seconds, the stamp the record was chained at. It has to equal the `iat` the receipt itself attests: the store chains a receipt under the stamp it was handed, so a reader who checked the walk and not this equality would accept a receipt moved into a window it was never issued in.

prev.description: the digest of the record before this one, or the anchor for the first item

receipt.description: the signed receipt bytes, whole and unaltered, exactly as the record's payload holds them. Each entry verifies on its own as `receipt-v1.schema.json` describes it, and this container adds nothing to what a receipt attests.

item.description: One receipt with the three values its record was hashed with, which is all it takes to rebuild that record's frame: the kind byte is 0 for every item, the id length and the record length count bytes that follow them, and the digest the next item names is sha256 over the kind, the predecessor digest, `iat` as eight big-endian bytes, the id length as two big-endian bytes, the id and the receipt bytes.

k.description: Which sealed receipt and which half of its anchor this reference answers for. The slot is the only name a reference is reached by, and an entry naming a slot no sealed receipt states is a record of an observation nobody asked it to stand behind.

o.description: The origin declaration this read, by the name that declaration states for itself. This projection names no set of them, and the reader of the container names none either, because a pack states which declaration was read and never holds the list a name is looked up in: an origin this build cannot reach is refused where a declaration is actually fetched, in `packages/collateral/src/intel-origin.ts`, and not here.

u.description: The request as it was asked, path and query members included. The CBOR bounds this text at 2048 bytes, which is the figure `pack.cddl` states for it rather than a number written in two places; a JSON string length cannot state a byte bound, so the ceiling lives there and this projection names no number for it.

i.description: The identity the document named for itself, such as the CPU it is about, or null where the answer names none. It is the document's own statement, spelled as the origin declaration's `identity` states it, and a projection that checked it against a firmware figure would be checking a fact it has no firmware to compare with.

s.description: Unix seconds, the instant the document's last byte landed on the clock that run was given. It is not a reading of any clock this file owns, and a millisecond spelling of the same instant lies outside the band the format states by a factor of a thousand, which is why the band is checked before any member of the material is weighed.

n.description: What that source declares about itself, in the same seconds-or-null pair the receipt's own stamp disclosure carries, or null where the source states nothing. A projection can show the figure and can say nothing about whether the document it came from was still standing at `s`, which is the reader's question with its own pins and its own instant.

b.description: sha256 of the body exactly as it arrived. Nothing in the container holds that body, so no check here can run against it: this is the digest a reader with the bytes recomputes, and a disagreement is the attachment refusing itself rather than a projection noticing one.

c.description: sha256 of the issuer-chain header exactly as it arrived beside that body, or null where no header arrived. This is the member that decides whether a chain has to come with the bytes, and it is a digest rather than a second run of bytes because a chain's own bytes are no member of this container: the header is the service's response, and a reference says what it hashed to without handing it on.

a.description: Which arm weighed the document at capture: `served` where the issuer chain arrived in a header beside the body, `embedded` where the certificates sit inside the document itself. It is the declaration's own answer rather than a guess from the bytes, and a reader that inferred it from a shape it could see would be reporting an opinion about a service's response as a fact the container states.

w.description: The window the document stated for itself, in the vendor's own signed words. A projection can show the two ends and can check neither against the document that signed them.

y.description: The cache key, spelled from the origin declaration's `cache.keyMembers`, so a reader that holds these bytes in its own store can find them again under the name the declaration gives them. It is derived from the request and the identity rather than stated beside them, and a second name for one material is the thing that drifts.

custody.description: One reference: what a sealed receipt's held slot was reached against, stated without the material and without a verdict on it. A projection shows each member and enforces none of the relations between them, which are the reader's and are stated in `pack.cddl`.

item.description: The id the pack gives the record whose anchor states the slot. The framing bounds it at 65535 bytes, which is the ceiling `item.id` carries and the reason this row states no number.

slot.description: Which half of that receipt's anchor the reference answers for: `col` for the signed collateral, `val` for the validity context. Two per record, which is the whole of what the count of references is bounded against.

custodyKey.description: The slot one reference answers for, named by the record and by the half of its anchor. Neither is derivable from the other, and a key of either alone would leave the reader guessing which of the two the entry meant.

from.description: Unix seconds, the instant the document says it began to stand.

to.description: Unix seconds, the instant it says it stops being read as standing.

window.description: The window the document signed for itself, in the order it signs it. Both ends are the vendor's statement carried through the reference, and whether the statement stood at the instant a reader asks about is settled by that reader's own pins, which this projection has none of.

bytes.description: The material, whole, exactly as it arrived, where a deployment attaches it. The CBOR bounds this run of bytes at 65535, which is the largest byte count the container already states, the one `id` is bounded at because the framing spends two bytes on its length; a JSON string length cannot state a byte bound, so the ceiling lives in `pack.cddl` and this projection names no number for it.

sha256.description: sha256 of the bytes beside it. The reader recomputes it and refuses a disagreement, which is what makes the entry a statement about its own bytes rather than a label over bytes the reader cannot see; a projection can show both halves of the pair and can check neither against the other.

chain.description: The issuer-chain header that arrived beside those bytes, exactly as it arrived, or null where none did. It is present exactly when the digest below is, and a header arriving with no digest stated for it is a document contradicting itself before any of its members are believed.

chain_sha256.description: sha256 of that header, or null where there was no header. The reader recomputes it, refuses a disagreement, and refuses a header carried here beside a reference whose `c` states none: the reference is what says whether a chain has to arrive at all. The label is spelled lowercase because every label this format writes is, and this projection names the label rather than the object field a caller of `@ashaveri/receipt` reads.

attached.description: One entry of the byte arm: material a deployment holds rights to hand on, stated as its bytes and as the digest of those bytes, beside the header that arrived with them and its digest. Resolution, the refusal of a stated digest that disagrees with its bytes, the refusal of a digest attached twice, the refusal of an entry no reference names and the refusal of a header no reference states a digest for are all stated in `pack.cddl` and enforced by the reader that recomputes them; this projection names both and performs neither.
